d: Unadulterated, pure, guileless.

e.t: This word means “pure,” describing something free from mixture, corruption, or deceit. It points to a clean and genuine quality rather than something tainted or falsely presented. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 2:2, so its exact force there is understood from the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains straightforward: what is pure is unspoiled and sincere, with nothing corrupting its character.

e.t: This word refers to a cause or reason, and it can also describe a case or charge brought before someone. It names the matter or grounds being considered, whether explaining why something happened or stating what someone is accused of. The Greek New Testament uses it 20 times, so its exact English expression depends on whether the context emphasizes a reason, a legal matter, or an accusation. Its central idea remains the cause or issue at hand.

e.t: This word means “true.” It describes something as genuinely true rather than false or deceptive. In the Greek New Testament, it is an adjective used to identify what is true in statements, descriptions, or declarations. It occurs 28 times across 26 verses, including several uses in John and Revelation. Its exact force in any particular verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

d: To examine, inquire into, investigate, question.

e.t: This word means “to examine” or “to investigate.” It describes looking into a matter carefully in order to determine what is true or what has happened. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, including settings involving questioning, inquiry, and the careful testing of claims. Its basic idea is active investigation rather than merely noticing something. The surrounding passage determines what is being examined and why, but the word itself points to deliberate inquiry aimed at finding out the facts.

d: Unholy, profane.
me: Adjective, Dative, Plural, Masculine
Adjective, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: “Unholy” describes a person or thing that is not holy—outside what is sacred, pure, or worthy of reverence toward God. It identifies a condition or character that does not honor holiness. This Greek New Testament word occurs twice, once in 1 Timothy and once in 2 Timothy, and is rendered “unholy” in both recorded passages. Its exact force in either verse is clarified by the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a description of what is unholy rather than devoted to what is holy.

d: Demonstration, proof; a showing off.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “demonstration”: a clear showing or proof of something. It describes an act that makes a matter evident rather than merely asserting it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 2:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but the central idea remains a visible or convincing showing. The word therefore points readers toward something presented in a way that allows its reality or truth to be recognized.

d: To have been put away, to be stored, to be reserved for.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to be stored up” or “to lay up.” It describes something reserved, kept, or set aside rather than immediately used. The word can point to something held in readiness for a later time, including what is preserved or awaiting its appointed outcome. It occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in Luke, Colossians, 2 Timothy, and Hebrews. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

d: To cause to disappear, hide, remove; to disfigure (probably by leaving unwashed for a long period), destroy.

Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to destroy,” describing the removal, ruin, or disappearance of something. It is a Greek New Testament verb and occurs five times, including passages that speak of outward religious appearance, earthly treasure, a future event announced by the prophets, and the brevity of human life. These settings show that the word can describe something being ruined or brought to an end, whether referring to possessions, appearances, expectations, or life itself. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

d: Bosor, father of Balaam.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word is a proper name, referring to “Beor,” also rendered “Bosor.” It is not an ordinary descriptive term or action word, but a personal name preserved in the Greek New Testament. It occurs once in that corpus, in 2 Peter 2:15. Since the available wording identifies the name rather than defining a broader concept, its meaning is simply the person-name represented by these two forms.

d: A waiter, servant; then of any one who performs any service, an administrator.

e.t: This word means “servant” or “servants”—a person who serves another. In the New Testament, it can describe ordinary service as well as a person identified by a serving role. Its meaning centers on serving rather than ruling or seeking status. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of serving others and serving Christ. The surrounding verse determines the particular setting, but the basic idea remains a servant who carries out service for someone else.

e.t: This word means to accuse someone or bring charges against them. It describes the act of making a formal complaint or alleging wrongdoing, especially in a legal or public setting. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, mostly in Acts, where accusations and charges are discussed before authorities. It can also describe the prospect of someone bringing an accusation. The central idea is a charge directed against a person, rather than a general statement of disagreement or criticism.

d: To narrate at length, declare.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to tell” or “to tell in detail.” It describes giving an account or report, with the wording capable of emphasizing a fuller, more detailed telling rather than a bare statement. It is a verb, so it expresses the act of communicating information. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains reporting or recounting something clearly and fully.

e.t: This word means “to show”—to make something visible, evident, or openly demonstrated. It describes the act of presenting something so that others can recognize or observe it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, including uses rendered “show” and “showing.” Its focus is not merely possessing something, but bringing it forward for others to see or acknowledge. The surrounding passage determines what is being shown and why, while the central idea remains clear: making something known through visible or expressed demonstration.

d: Suddenly, unexpectedly.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “suddenly,” describing something that happens abruptly or without advance warning. It functions as an adverb, telling when an action or event occurs rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, including passages in Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its basic force remains consistent: an event occurs all at once, catching attention because it was not gradually developing in view. The surrounding verse determines what happens suddenly, but this word emphasizes the unexpected timing of the event.

d: Life, both of physical (present) and of spiritual (particularly future) existence.

e.t: This word means “life,” referring to living existence and the condition of being alive. In the Greek New Testament, it is used broadly, including statements about receiving life, possessing life, losing life, and seeking life. Its repeated use—135 occurrences—shows that life is a significant subject throughout the New Testament, especially in John and Revelation. The exact force in any passage depends on its surrounding words and context.

d: (Hebrew), Jonah, the Hebrew prophet.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: “Jonah” is a personal name used to identify a man in the Greek New Testament. It refers to the person named Jonah rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs nine times in seven New Testament verses, concentrated in Matthew and Luke. Its repeated use in passages concerning a sign shows that Jonah is treated as a recognizable biblical person whose name could be used as a reference point for readers.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 22 times, including several passages in Matthew describing people who were asleep and others in which sleep is contrasted with wakefulness. Its basic sense remains straightforward: being in a natural state of sleep rather than being awake.

In the New Testament, it can describe God as the Creator and can also describe the making of something new. Its meaning centers on originating, forming, or producing rather than merely changing something that already exists. e.t: This word means to take or receive something. It can describe accepting what is offered, taking hold of something, or receiving what is given. Its wording may be rendered as “take,” “received,” “takes,” or “taking,” depending on the sentence. It is a common Greek New Testament word, occurring 258 times, so its precise force depends on what is being taken or received and the surrounding statement. It appears throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. [p03:word:greek-nt:G2983:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G2983:occurrences]

d: Finally, from now on, henceforth, beyond that.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “henceforth” or “remaining.” It marks what follows as continuing from a certain point onward, or identifies what is left. Thus, it can direct attention to the time still ahead or to something that remains. It occurs 13 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing across several books, so its basic sense serves both time-related and remainder-related statements. The surrounding sentence determines which aspect is most prominent in a particular verse.

d: Long, distant, far; of long duration.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Neuter
Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word describes something distant or far away, and it can also express something long in extent or duration. Its central idea is considerable distance—whether physical space separates people or a stretch of time or length is involved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, with “distant,” “far away,” “lengthy,” and “long” expressing its recognized range of meaning. The surrounding sentence determines whether the distance is spatial or the length is extended.

d: A bird, fowl, hen.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “hen,” referring to a female chicken. It is a noun used for the bird itself, rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: in Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34. Both occurrences are rendered “hen,” confirming this straightforward meaning. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains the common term for a hen.

d: Advantage, gain, profit, help.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word refers to gain or something good—that is, a benefit or advantage. It describes what is profitable or worthwhile rather than merely something that exists. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times: once in 1 Corinthians and twice in James. Its use in James is connected with asking what “good” comes from words or claims that do not provide practical help. The surrounding verse determines the particular kind of benefit being discussed.

d: A falling away, lapse, slip, false step, trespass, sin.

e.t: This word means “trespass” or “trespasses,” referring to a wrong act or offense. It names conduct that violates what is right and therefore creates guilt or liability before God or another person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times, including teaching about forgiving trespasses and describing human wrongdoing in Romans and Ephesians. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a trespass: a failure or transgression that requires forgiveness or correction.

d: To leave behind; pass: to be left behind, remain, survive.
me: Verb, Present, passive depOnent, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to be left” or “to remain.” It describes people who are still present after others have departed, or those who continue in place rather than being taken away. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Thessalonians 4:15 and 4:17. Its basic sense is straightforward: someone is left behind or continues to remain. The surrounding passage determines which aspect is emphasized in a particular verse.

d: An officer employed to execute judicial sentences.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Masculine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “bailiff” or “officer,” referring to an official who carries out authority or legal action. It identifies a person serving in an official role rather than describing a general crowd or ordinary worker. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse, Luke 12:58. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is an officer or bailiff.

d: A setting forth, the show-bread; predetermination, purpose.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “purpose” or “setting forth”—an intended aim, plan, or deliberate arrangement. It is used as a noun, describing what is planned or set before someone rather than an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times in 12 verses, including passages translated with the word “purpose.” Its range includes a stated intention and something placed or arranged for a particular use. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent, but the central idea remains a settled aim or an intentional setting before others.

d: To stumble, fall, sin, err, transgress.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to stumble.” It describes the act of stumbling and functions as a verb in a sentence. The word appears five times in four New Testament verses, including Romans 11:11, James 2:10 and 3:2, and 2 Peter 1:10. Its basic meaning remains focused and consistent across these occurrences: a person or group stumbles. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to a literal or figurative stumbling, but the central idea is falling into difficulty or failing to proceed steadily.

d: To sweep, cleanse by sweeping.
me: Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to sweep,” describing the action of sweeping a place. It refers to clearing or cleaning by moving unwanted material away with a sweeping motion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, so its basic meaning is consistent but its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding context. The word appears in Matthew and Luke, including the account of a woman sweeping her house to find a lost coin.

d: A babbler, gossiper, one who picks up seeds and trifles as does a bird.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: “Babbler” refers to a person whose speech is viewed as scattered, trivial, or lacking substantial sense. It is a noun used as a label for someone known for this kind of talk, rather than a description of an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at Acts 17:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a dismissive name for a talker.

d: To throw violently on the ground.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to cause to convulse” or “to convulse.” It describes violent, uncontrolled bodily movement, either as something happening to a person or as an action causing such movement. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 9:20 and Luke 9:42. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains convulsive movement rather than ordinary motion or discomfort.

d: Then, at that time.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “then”. It points to a time or event that follows another point in the account, helping readers see sequence and movement. It may introduce what happened next, what someone did afterward, or what a future situation will be like. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 160 times, showing that it is a common word for organizing events and statements in time. Its exact force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: A water pot, jar, pitcher.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Feminine
Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Nominative, Plural, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means a jar, specifically a water jar. It refers to a container used for carrying or holding water, rather than to the water itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, all in John: twice in chapter 2 and once in chapter 4. Its ordinary meaning is therefore a physical vessel associated with water, and the surrounding verse determines its particular role in each occurrence.

d: (a) to take up, (b) to welcome, entertain, (c) to answer, (d) to suppose, imagine.

e.t: This word can mean “to suppose,” “to receive,” “to take up,” or “to catch up in speech.” Its central idea depends on what is being taken up: it may express accepting something, forming an understanding, or responding in speech. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, so its meaning is shown across a small number of passages rather than through a broad range of repeated uses. The precise sense in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

d: High, lofty.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: This word means “high,” describing something elevated in position or loftiness rather than low or near the ground. It is used in the Greek New Testament as a descriptive word, and its ordinary sense remains focused on height or elevation. The word occurs 11 times across 11 New Testament verses, showing that it can describe different people, places, or things according to their setting. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

d: A gap, gulf, chasm.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “chasm,” referring to a deep gap or divide that separates one side from another. It describes a separation that is not easily crossed or bridged. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 16:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on the idea of a broad, impassable separation rather than a small crack or ordinary distance.

d: To furnish abundantly, supply.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to provide” or “to supply,” describing the act of furnishing what is needed. It can refer to God supplying something for fruitful work, or to believers supplying strength and help through what God gives them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Corinthians 9:10 and 1 Peter 4:11. Its basic sense is active provision: something is supplied so that another person, work, or purpose can be supported.

d: To waste time, spend time, delay.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive

e.h: A Word for To Spend Time
e.t: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. Its basic sense is “to spend time”. It describes using or allowing time to pass, without by itself explaining whether that time is used wisely, wastefully, patiently, or urgently. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 20:16. Its meaning remains focused on the expenditure of time rather than on a broader spiritual or emotional idea.

me: Verb, second Aorist, Passive, iMperative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to be changed” or “to turn around.” It describes a person or situation being altered from its present condition or direction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 4:9. These two related meanings present change as a real turning or reversal rather than merely remaining as before. The surrounding verse is needed to show precisely how that change is expressed there.
